pos: n. phr. (the gladness proper to a pardoned sinner, asked back after sin)
etymology: Hebrew sason yesha' — sason, exultation or rejoicing, and yesha', deliverance or salvation; the construct names the gladness that belongs to being saved, not a mood manufactured apart from it.
biblical_def: David's fifty-first Psalm is the penitential prayer of a believing man after adultery and murder, and the petition at its centre is exact: “Restore unto me the joy of thy salvation; and uphold me with thy free spirit.” Three things in the asking govern the doctrine. First, the joy is thy salvation's joy — it is God's saving work that produces it, so it cannot be worked up by the sinner who lost it. Second, what he asks for is restoration, not a first granting; the salvation itself was never in question, only the felt gladness of it, which sin had driven off as surely as a hand smothers a flame. Third, the petition sits between a plea for a clean heart and a vow to teach transgressors God's ways, which is to say that recovered joy is not an end in itself but the strength of a restored man's usefulness. The verse is therefore the Psalter's clearest witness that a true child of God may lose the comfort of his salvation while never losing the salvation, and that the way back is not self-reproach but petition. Assurance and joy, the Reformed divines distinguished carefully, are fruits of faith and not its essence; they may be shaken, and they are restored where they were first given, by asking at the throne of grace.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): Joy, the passion or emotion excited by the acquisition or expectation of good; gladness, exultation. Salvation, the redemption of man from sin and liability to eternal death. The joy of thy salvation, Psalm 51:12, the gladness proper to a pardoned sinner.
webster_full: Joy, the passion excited by the acquisition or expectation of good; gladness.
Salvation, the redemption of man from sin and the liability to eternal death.
Hebrew sason, exultation or rejoicing, often of festival gladness.
Hebrew yesha', deliverance, help, or salvation wrought by another.
Restore unto me the joy of thy salvation, Psalm 51:12.
scriptures: Restore unto me the joy of thy salvation; and uphold me with thy free spirit.
Create in me a clean heart, O God; and renew a right spirit within me.
The sacrifices of God are a broken spirit: a broken and a contrite heart, O God, thou wilt not despise.
Psa 32:1
A Psalm of David, Maschil. Blessed is he whose transgression is forgiven, whose sin is covered.
corruption_summary: The petition is recast as a request for an emotional experience detached from pardon, or else pressed to prove that a man who has lost his joy has lost his salvation.
corruption_paragraphs: The modern worship register treats joy as an atmosphere to be produced — a room, a volume, a swell of music — and so reads David as asking for a feeling rather than for the gladness that pardon itself carries with it. The Psalm forbids the substitution. What David asks for stands beside a clean heart, a right spirit, washing, blotting out, and bones that God had broken; it is the joy of a salvation, and it comes back only as the salvation is freshly tasted in forgiveness. A gladness got up by other means is not this joy, and it will not survive the next sin.

The opposite error turns the verse into a test of standing: if a man has no joy, he was never saved. Scripture does not reason that way. David is a regenerate man under the Spirit's conviction, and the Psalter is full of the same voice asking why his soul is cast down. The 1689 Confession says plainly that true believers may have the light of God's countenance withdrawn for a season and yet are never utterly destitute of that seed of God and life of faith. The principle to recover is the pastoral one: a joyless believer is to be sent to petition, not to despair.
roots_summary: Hebrew sason, exultation; yesha', deliverance; shub in the hiphil, to cause to return, hence restore — the joy comes back by God's act, as it came first.
roots_lines: Hebrew sason, exultation, rejoicing, the gladness of a festival.
Hebrew yesha', deliverance or salvation wrought by God for a man.
Hebrew shub (hiphil), to cause to return — hence ‘restore unto me’.
Hebrew ruach nedibah, a free or willing spirit, the upholding asked beside it.
Set between a clean heart (Psalm 51:10) and teaching transgressors (Psalm 51:13).

pos: n. phr. (in the Preacher's figure of dying, the cord whose loosing ends the lamp's service)
etymology: Hebrew chebel ha-keseph — chebel, a rope or cord, and keseph, silver; the figure is a hanging lamp, suspended by a costly cord over a bowl of oil, and the loosing of the cord is the breaking of the lamp.
biblical_def: Ecclesiastes closes its long argument with an allegory of old age and death, and the first of its four images is the suspended lamp: “Or ever the silver cord be loosed, or the golden bowl be broken, or the pitcher be broken at the fountain, or the wheel broken at the cistern.” The Preacher has been urging a young man to remember his Creator in the days of his youth, and these are the reasons — four pictures of a serviceable thing put permanently out of use. The lamp hangs by a cord of silver over a bowl of gold; cut the cord and both are ruined together, the light gone in an instant. The water vessel shatters at the spring, the wheel that drew it breaks at the cistern, and the household that drank is dry. Each figure says the same thing twice over: the end does not mend, and it comes while the fountain is still flowing. The verse that follows removes any doubt as to the subject, for it names dust returning to the earth and the spirit returning to God who gave it. The silver cord is therefore not a mystical tether of body to soul, as later esoteric writers made it, but the Preacher's plain and beautiful way of saying that a man's life is a lamp held up by a thread.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): Cord, a string, or small rope, composed of several strands twisted together. Silver, a metal of a white colour, the most ductile and malleable after gold. The silver cord, Ecclesiastes 12:6, in the Preacher's figure, the thread by which the lamp of life hangs.
webster_full: Cord, a string or small rope composed of several strands twisted together.
Silver, a white metal, ductile and malleable, valued next after gold.
Hebrew chebel, a rope, cord, or line, also a measured portion.
Hebrew keseph, silver, and by metonymy money or price.
The silver cord loosed, the golden bowl broken, Ecclesiastes 12:6.
scriptures: Ecc 12:6
Or ever the silver cord be loosed, or the golden bowl be broken, or the pitcher be broken at the fountain, or the wheel broken at the cistern.
Ecc 12:7
Then shall the dust return to the earth as it was: and the spirit shall return unto God who gave it.
Ecc 12:1
Remember now thy Creator in the days of thy youth, while the evil days come not, nor the years draw nigh, when thou shalt say, I have no pleasure in them;
So teach us to number our days, that we may apply our hearts unto wisdom.
corruption_summary: Theosophical and New Age writing seized the phrase for an astral tether joining soul to body, a sense the Preacher's own figure and following verse exclude.
corruption_paragraphs: Nineteenth-century theosophy and the occult revival that followed it made the silver cord a literal luminous tether by which a travelling soul remains joined to its sleeping body, and the phrase is still used that way in books on out-of-body experience. The borrowing is purely verbal. Ecclesiastes 12:6 stands in a series of four domestic objects — cord, bowl, pitcher, wheel — every one of them a vessel or fitting that breaks and is done with, and the next verse states the two destinations plainly: the dust to the earth, the spirit to God who gave it. There is no roaming soul in the passage and no cord to bring one home.

A quieter error empties the figure of its urgency by reading the chapter as a melancholy meditation on mortality and nothing more. The Preacher is not musing; he is pressing a command. Remember now thy Creator in the days of thy youth, or ever the cord be loosed — the whole weight of the image falls on the word before. The principle to recover is that the certainty of death is given to us as a reason to act early, and that the fear of God and the keeping of His commandments, which the book names as the whole duty of man, are matters for the strong years and not the failing ones.
roots_summary: Hebrew chebel, cord or rope; keseph, silver; gullah, a bowl or round vessel — a hanging lamp, costly in its fittings and instantly ruined when the cord parts.
roots_lines: Hebrew chebel, a cord, rope, or line by which a thing is held.
Hebrew keseph, silver, the metal and by extension money or price.
Hebrew gullah, a bowl or round vessel, here the lamp's golden reservoir.
Hebrew nathaq (niphal), to be snapped, torn apart, or loosed asunder.
First of four breaking-vessel figures; dust and spirit part in Ecclesiastes 12:7.

pos: n. phr. (in the Preacher's picture of age, the least weight grown heavy)
etymology: Hebrew chagab, a locust or grasshopper, with sabal, to bear a load; the figure weighs the lightest creature in the field against the strength of a man in his last years.
biblical_def: In the Preacher's allegory of old age the failures are catalogued one by one — the keepers of the house tremble, the grinders cease because they are few, those that look out of the windows are darkened — and then the reach of the picture widens: “Also when they shall be afraid of that which is high, and fears shall be in the way, and the almond tree shall flourish, and the grasshopper shall be a burden, and desire shall fail.” A grasshopper weighs nothing. That is precisely the point of naming it. The strength that once bore sheaves cannot now bear the weight of a locust, and a flight of stairs has become a height to dread. The almond tree flourishing is the white blossom of a head gone grey; desire failing is the quiet going out of appetite itself. The Preacher is not mocking the aged, and nothing in the chapter sneers. He is doing for his young reader what no young reader does for himself: setting the end of strength plainly in view while there is still strength to spend. Scripture elsewhere honours the hoary head as a crown of glory, and the same Preacher commands that the Creator be remembered before these days come, which is to say that the picture is drawn to produce early obedience, not late regret.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): Grasshopper, an insect of the genus Gryllus, which lives among grass. Burden, that which is borne or carried; a load. The grasshopper shall be a burden, Ecclesiastes 12:5, the least weight grown heavy to the aged.
webster_full: Grasshopper, an insect of the genus Gryllus, living among grass, of light body.
Burden, that which is borne or carried; a load; hence anything grievous to bear.
Hebrew chagab, a grasshopper or locust, one of the smaller clean creatures.
Hebrew sabal, to bear a load, to carry a weight laid upon one.
Set beside the flourishing almond tree and failing desire, Ecclesiastes 12:5.
scriptures: Ecc 12:5

Also when they shall be afraid of that which is high, and fears shall be in the way, and the almond tree shall flourish, and the grasshopper shall be a burden, and desire shall fail: because man goeth to his long home, and the mourners go about the streets:
Ecc 12:3
In the day when the keepers of the house shall tremble, and the strong men shall bow themselves, and the grinders cease because they are few, and those that look out of the windows be darkened,
Ecc 12:1
Remember now thy Creator in the days of thy youth, while the evil days come not, nor the years draw nigh, when thou shalt say, I have no pleasure in them;
The days of our years are threescore years and ten; and if by reason of strength they be fourscore years, yet is their strength labour and sorrow; for it is soon cut off, and we fly away.
corruption_summary: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition; the loss is rather that a culture which hides its aged no longer hears the verse at all.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The phrase has no contested theological history and no rival reading worth naming. What it has suffered is neglect, and of a particular kind. A society that moves its old people out of sight loses the only teachers who could make Ecclesiastes 12 intelligible, and a young man who has never watched strength fail reads the chapter as poetry about someone else.

The principle to recover is the Preacher's own order. He names the failures not to shame the weak but to date the command: remember thy Creator in the days of thy youth, while the grasshopper is still nothing. Scripture couples this with the honour owed to age — the hoary head is a crown of glory, and the fifth commandment reaches to grey hairs — so the right use of this verse is twofold. It presses the young to spend their best years on God, and it sends them to the aged in their churches and households rather than away from them, since the burden of the grasshopper is a thing to be helped and not merely observed.

word: Cast Thy Bread Upon the Waters
pronunciation: KAST thy BRED uh-PON thuh WAW-terz
pos: v. phr. (the Preacher's charge to give and to venture without seeing the return)
etymology: Hebrew shalach lachmeka al penei ha-mayim — shalach, to send out or let go; lechem, bread or food; the margin reads “upon the face of the waters,” the idiom of a merchant's grain sent out by sea.
biblical_def: “Cast thy bread upon the waters: for thou shalt find it after many days.” Two readings of the figure have been held by sound men and neither excludes the other. The first is commercial: a man sends his grain out in ships, loses sight of it entirely, and is repaid long after — the venture of honest trade, which must act before it can see. The second is the charitable, and it is the one the Jewish and Puritan expositors chiefly pressed: a man gives his bread away where he can expect nothing back, scattering it as seed upon water, and God sees that he finds it again. The verses that follow hold both together, commanding that seed be sown in the morning and in the evening because the sower does not know which will prosper, and warning that he who watches the clouds and the wind will never sow at all. This is the Preacher's answer to his own book. Having proved that a man cannot see the whole, that times and chances are hidden from him, he does not conclude in paralysis but in open-handed action under providence. The one thing a man may not do with an unknown future is nothing.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): Cast, to throw, to send or drive by force. Bread, food in general; the staff of life. Cast thy bread upon the waters, Ecclesiastes 11:1, give and venture freely, trusting God for the return.
webster_full: Cast, to throw, fling, or send forth by the hand or by force.
Bread, food made of ground grain; in Scripture, food in general, sustenance.
Hebrew shalach, to send out, let go, or dismiss from the hand.
Hebrew lechem, bread, food, or grain, the ordinary word for daily provision.
Sow in the morning and in the evening, for thou knowest not, Ecclesiastes 11:6.
scriptures: Ecc 11:1
Cast thy bread upon the waters: for thou shalt find it after many days.
Ecc 11:6
In the morning sow thy seed, and in the evening withhold not thine hand: for thou knowest not whether shall prosper, either this or that, or whether they both shall be alike good.
The liberal soul shall be made fat: and he that watereth shall be watered also himself.
Gal 6:9
And let us not be weary in well doing: for in due season we shall reap, if we faint not.
corruption_summary: The verse is pressed into a prosperity formula in which giving is an investment with a guaranteed and measurable yield, which inverts the Preacher's whole argument about what man cannot see.
corruption_paragraphs: The seed-faith teaching of the prosperity movement quotes this verse constantly, and always in the one sense the context will not bear: give a sum, name the return, expect it. The Preacher says the opposite. His reason for commanding the scattering is that the giver does not know — not which sowing will prosper, not what the day will bring, not the way of the spirit nor how the bones grow. “After many days” is deliberately indefinite, and the book's refrain is that a man cannot find out the work of God from beginning to end. A promise of measurable yield in exchange for a gift is not this verse's doctrine; it is the merchandising of godliness the apostle told Timothy to withdraw from.

A second and opposite failure reads Ecclesiastes 11 as fatalism — all is vanity, the outcome is hidden, so why sow? The chapter answers that objection directly in the fourth verse: he that observeth the wind shall not sow, and he that regardeth the clouds shall not reap. The principle to recover is the one the Reformed have always drawn from providence, that confidence in God's hidden government is the warrant for diligence rather than an excuse from it. The sower gives in the morning and again in the evening, and leaves the increase where it has always belonged.

pos: n. phr. (the storehouses of snow and hail which the LORD keeps, named to Job out of the whirlwind)
etymology: Hebrew otserot ha-sheleg — otsar, a treasury, storehouse, or armoury, and sheleg, snow; the figure is a royal magazine whose doors only the Owner opens.
biblical_def: When the LORD answers Job out of the whirlwind He does not explain Job's suffering. He asks questions, and one of them is this: “Hast thou entered into the treasures of the snow? or hast thou seen the treasures of the hail?” The word rendered treasures is the word for a king's storehouse or an armoury, and the next clause names the use to which this particular magazine is put — reserved against the day of battle and war. Snow and hail, which to a man are weather, are to God stock kept under lock for a purpose he has not been shown and could not inspect. The force of the question is not that Job is ignorant of meteorology but that he has been arguing about the government of the world with One who keeps arsenals Job has never entered. Scripture presses the same point elsewhere by narrative: hail fought for Israel at Beth-horon, and the plague of hail broke Egypt. The Reformed doctrine of providence stands squarely here. There is no realm of mere nature running on its own; the very snow has a steward, a storehouse, and an appointed day, and the creature's proper answer is the one Job finally gives, that he had heard by the hearing of the ear but now his eye seeth.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): Treasure, wealth accumulated; a great quantity of anything collected for future use. Snow, water fallen from the clouds in congealed flakes. The treasures of the snow, Job 38:22, God's storehouses of snow and hail.
webster_full: Treasure, wealth accumulated, or a store of anything laid up for future use.
Snow, water in the atmosphere congealed into flakes and falling to the earth.
Hebrew otsar, a treasury, storehouse, magazine, or armoury.
Hebrew sheleg, snow; and barad, hail, named with it in the same verse.
Reserved against the day of battle and war, Job 38:23.
scriptures: Hast thou entered into the treasures of the snow? or hast thou seen the treasures of the hail,
Which I have reserved against the time of trouble, against the day of battle and war?
Job 38:4
Where wast thou when I laid the foundations of the earth? declare, if thou hast understanding.
Job 42:5
I have heard of thee by the hearing of the ear: but now mine eye seeth thee.
corruption_summary: A closed naturalism grants the weather its own self-contained causes and leaves no room for a storehouse with an Owner, which is exactly the claim the whirlwind speech denies.
corruption_paragraphs: The governing assumption of the modern account of weather is that the system is closed — fully described by its own mechanism, with nothing left for God to do but watch. Scripture does not dispute the mechanism and never did; the Hebrew knew that snow falls from clouds. What it denies is the closure. The whirlwind speech addresses snow and hail as stores held against an appointed day, which is a statement about government and purpose, not about physics, and no measurement of a cloud can touch it. A Christian may learn the mechanism gladly and still answer Job's question with the only honest answer: he has not entered those treasuries.

The second failure is nearer home. Much popular Christian writing takes up this chapter as a lesson in human smallness and stops there, as though the point were that Job should feel little. The chapter aims higher. Every question put to Job has an implied answer in God's own competence — He laid the foundations, He shut the sea with doors, He keeps the snow — so that the result is not the crushing of a sufferer but the resting of one. The principle to recover is that God's government of the least thing is the ground of a believer's peace about the worst thing.

word: The Way of an Eagle in the Air
pronunciation: thuh WAY uv an EE-gul in thee AIR
pos: n. phr. (first of Agur's four trackless ways, too wonderful for him)
etymology: Hebrew derek ha-nesher ba-shamayim — derek, a way, road, or course; nesher, the eagle or great vulture; shamayim, the heavens; the common note of Agur's four is that each leaves no track behind it.
biblical_def: Agur the son of Jakeh names four things too wonderful for him and then lists them: “The way of an eagle in the air; the way of a serpent upon a rock; the way of a ship in the midst of the sea; and the way of a man with a maid.” Commentators have proposed several unifying notes, but the plainest is the one the pictures share: not one of the four leaves a mark. The eagle crosses the sky and the sky closes behind it; the serpent passes over bare rock without print or trail; the ship's wake heals; and the way of a man with a maid, the courting that joins two lives, goes on in a secrecy no observer can chart. Agur is a wise man confessing a limit, which is the posture the whole book commends, and the next verse turns the figure to its moral use: so is the way of the adulterous woman, who eateth and wipeth her mouth and saith, I have done no wickedness. The tracklessness that is wonder in the eagle is cover for sin in her. The passage therefore does two things at once — it humbles the wise before creation's unreadable ways, and it warns that the sin which leaves no evidence is still seen by the One who weighs the heart.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): Way, a passing; a course; the manner in which anything is done. Eagle, a rapacious fowl of the genus Falco. The way of an eagle in the air, Proverbs 30:19, first of the four trackless ways Agur calls too wonderful.
webster_full: Way, a passing or course; also the manner or method in which a thing is done.
Eagle, a large rapacious fowl, of swift and lofty flight.
Hebrew derek, a way, road, journey, or habitual course of acting.
Hebrew nesher, the eagle or great vulture, noted for height and speed.
Named with the serpent, the ship, and the man with a maid, Proverbs 30:19.
scriptures: The way of an eagle in the air; the way of a serpent upon a rock; the way of a ship in the midst of the sea; and the way of a man with a maid.
There be three things which are too wonderful for me, yea, four which I know not:
Such is the way of an adulterous woman; she eateth, and wipeth her mouth, and saith, I have done no wickedness.
Jer 17:9
The heart is deceitful above all things, and desperately wicked: who can know it?
corruption_summary: The sayings of Agur are treated as folk curiosities detachable from the chapter's doctrine of God, and the warning the figure is drawn for is quietly dropped.
corruption_paragraphs: Proverbs 30 is commonly handled as an anthology of numerical folk sayings, charming and more or less free-standing, which lets a reader enjoy the eagle and skip what the chapter is for. Agur does not permit it. He opens by confessing that he is more brutish than any man and has not the knowledge of the Holy, asks who hath ascended up into heaven and what is his son's name, and declares every word of God pure and a shield to them that put their trust in him. The four wonders are set inside that frame. Read apart from it they become decoration; read within it they are a wise man's evidence that creation outruns him and that the fear of the LORD is where knowledge begins.

The sharper loss is the nineteenth verse's own sequel. Agur's point in gathering four trackless ways is to set beside them a fifth: the adulterous woman who eats, wipes her mouth, and says she has done no wickedness. Modern treatments of the chapter rarely reach her, and a sentimental reading of the eagle actually works against the text, since the wonder of leaving no trace becomes, in her mouth, the boast of concealment. The principle to recover is that secrecy is no acquittal. Scripture answers her claim with the heart that is deceitful above all things and with a God who searches it.

word: Sparrow Alone Upon the House Top
pronunciation: SPAR-oh uh-LOHN uh-PON thuh HOWS top
pos: n. phr. (the afflicted psalmist's figure of sleepless solitude)
etymology: Hebrew tsippor boded al gag — tsippor, a small bird or sparrow; badad, to be alone, separated, solitary; gag, a flat roof; the bird is pictured awake on the housetop while the household sleeps beneath it.
biblical_def: The hundred and second Psalm is headed a prayer of the afflicted, when he is overwhelmed, and poureth out his complaint before the LORD, and its images of loneliness are three birds: “I am like a pelican of the wilderness: I am like an owl of the desert. I watch, and am as a sparrow alone upon the house top.” The sparrow is the commonest bird in Scripture and the cheapest — two were sold for a farthing — and it is never alone; that is what makes the figure bite. A solitary sparrow on a flat Eastern roof, awake above a sleeping house, is the picture of a man cut off from the company that is natural to him and unable to rest. The verb rendered watch is the word for keeping vigil. What makes this Psalm more than a lament is where it turns. From the ashes and the withered grass of his own days the psalmist lifts his eyes: “But thou, O LORD, shalt endure for ever,” and the Spirit afterwards applies those very verses to the Son in the first chapter of Hebrews. The solitary bird is therefore not left on the roof. The Psalm places a sufferer's sleepless loneliness in the hands of an unchanging and eternal God, and the New Testament names that God as Christ.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): Sparrow, a small bird of the genus Fringilla. Alone, apart from others; single; solitary. A sparrow alone upon the house top, Psalm 102:7, the figure of a sleepless and solitary sufferer.
webster_full: Sparrow, a small bird of the genus Fringilla, common about houses.
Alone, apart from others, single, solitary, without company.
Hebrew tsippor, a small bird or sparrow, proverbially of little price.
Hebrew badad, to be separate or solitary, used of one set apart alone.
Hebrew gag, a flat housetop, the place of watching and of vigil.
scriptures: I watch, and am as a sparrow alone upon the house top.
I am like a pelican of the wilderness: I am like an owl of the desert.
My days are like a shadow that declineth; and I am withered like grass.
Are not two sparrows sold for a farthing? and one of them shall not fall on the ground without your Father.
corruption_summary: Therapeutic reading turns the Psalm into the validating of a feeling and stops before its turn, where the sufferer's eye moves from his own withering days to an unchanging God.
corruption_paragraphs: The lament psalms are now commonly commended for their usefulness in naming emotion, and Psalm 102 is quoted as far as the seventh verse to assure a reader that his loneliness is permitted. The permission is real and Scripture gives it freely; this Psalm is a prayer of the afflicted by its own title, and no Christian is required to pretend. But to stop at the sparrow is to read half a Psalm and to leave a sufferer where the Psalm refuses to leave him. The turn comes at the twelfth verse, and it is not a feeling about himself but a truth about God: thou, O LORD, shalt endure for ever. The cure of loneliness here is not acceptance of it but the eternity and compassion of the One addressed.

The second loss is the Psalm's Christology. Hebrews 1:10-12 takes the words of Psalm 102 about the founding of the earth and the perishing of the heavens and applies them directly to the Son, which means the afflicted man's prayer is answered by the identity of his hearer. The principle to recover is that biblical lament is addressed, and addressed to a Person who was Himself a man of sorrows and acquainted with grief. That is why the sparrow is the right image: the Lord who notices one of them falling to the ground is the Lord sitting awake on the roof.
roots_summary: Hebrew tsippor, sparrow; badad, to be solitary; gag, the flat roof; shaqad, to watch or keep vigil — a common bird out of its flock, awake above a sleeping house.

Hebrew shaqad, to watch, to be sleepless, to keep vigil through the night.

word: My Times Are in Thy Hand
pronunciation: my TYMZ ar in thy HAND
pos: n. phr. (David's confession that the seasons of his life are God's to appoint)
etymology: Hebrew be-yadeka ittothai — yad, the hand, the standard figure for power and disposal, and ittim, the plural of eth, appointed times or seasons; the plural is deliberate, covering not one hour but every turn of a life.
biblical_def: Hunted and slandered, David says, “But I trusted in thee, O LORD: I said, Thou art my God. My times are in thy hand: deliver me from the hand of mine enemies, and from them that persecute me.” The two hands in the sentence are the whole of its doctrine. The enemy has a hand and it is real; David asks to be delivered out of it. But his times are in another hand, and because they are, the enemy's hand reaches only so far as the LORD appoints. Note what David does not say. He does not claim to know his times, nor that they will be pleasant, nor that the persecution will end soon. He says they are held, and then he prays — which is the Reformed account of providence working itself out in a believing man's practice. The plural times matters. Scripture elsewhere speaks of a time to be born and a time to die, of the days of a man being determined, of the bounds of habitation appointed, and Christ Himself answered that His hour was not yet come. A man whose times are in God's hand is not thereby passive; David is actively asking, as the same verse shows. He is simply no longer at the mercy of accident, and that is what makes petition sane.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): Time, a particular portion or part of duration; season; the appointed hour. Hand, in Scripture, power, might, dominion. My times are in thy hand, Psalm 31:15, the confession that God appoints every season of a life.
webster_full: Time, a particular portion of duration; a season; the appointed or fit hour.
Hand, in Scripture, power, might, or dominion; that which disposes of a thing.
Hebrew eth, an appointed time or season, here in the plural, ittim.
Hebrew yad, the hand, the common figure for authority and disposal.
Set between trust confessed and deliverance asked, Psalm 31:14-15.
scriptures: My times are in thy hand: deliver me from the hand of mine enemies, and from them that persecute me.
But I trusted in thee, O LORD: I said, Thou art my God.
Job 14:5
Seeing his days are determined, the number of his months are with thee, thou hast appointed his bounds that he cannot pass;
And hath made of one blood all nations of men for to dwell on all the face of the earth, and hath determined the times before appointed, and the bounds of their habitation;
corruption_summary: The confession is flattened either into fatalism, which makes prayer pointless, or into a promise of favourable timing, which the verse never gives.
corruption_paragraphs: The open-theist account of God, which denies exhaustive foreknowledge and makes the future genuinely undetermined even for Him, cannot say this verse. Pinnock, Boyd and Sanders propose a God who learns as history unfolds, and a man whose times are in such a hand is held by a grip that does not yet know where it is going. Scripture's own language is otherwise: the days are determined, the number of the months is with Him, the bounds of habitation are appointed beforehand, and the Son's hour came at the Father's appointment and not a moment earlier. Nothing in David's comfort survives the subtraction of God's certain knowledge of his times.

On the other side the verse is used as an assurance that the timing will be good in the sense the sufferer means — relief soon, the trial short. David's own history refuses that reading; the same Psalm says his strength faileth and his years are consumed with grief, and the deliverance he asks for was years in coming. The principle to recover is the one the verse actually teaches. Because the times are held, the believer prays; he does not predict. Fatalism makes petition absurd, and sentimentality makes it a bargain, while David does the sane thing and asks.
roots_summary: Hebrew ittim, appointed times in the plural; yad, hand, the figure of disposal — the enemy's hand in the same verse reaches only as far as the LORD's hand permits.
roots_lines: Hebrew eth (plural ittim), an appointed time, season, or fit occasion.
Hebrew yad, hand; by metonymy power, authority, and the right of disposal.
The same verse sets God's hand against the hand of persecuting enemies.
Hebrew batach, to trust or lean upon, the verb of the preceding confession.
Compare the determined days and numbered months of Job 14:5.

word: Precious in the Sight of the LORD
pronunciation: PRESH-us in thuh SYT uv thuh LORD
pos: n. phr. (the value God sets upon the death of His saints)
etymology: Hebrew yaqar be-einei YHWH — yaqar, costly, weighty, held at a high price (used of precious stones and of blood not lightly spilt), with be-einei, in the eyes of; the idiom is of worth reckoned by a particular valuer.
biblical_def: “Precious in the sight of the LORD is the death of his saints.” The Psalm is a thanksgiving by a man who has himself been brought back from the gates of death — the sorrows of death compassed me, he says, and then, thou hast delivered my soul from death — and this verse is his verdict on the whole matter. The word rendered precious is the word for costly: a thing not spent carelessly, held at a price. God does not lose His saints cheaply or by accident. Their dying is reckoned, valued, and timed by Him, which is why the same Psalm can call the psalmist the son of God's handmaid and say that his bonds are loosed. Two consequences follow and the Reformed have pressed both. The first is comfort: no believer dies outside that reckoning, and the death that looks to onlookers like loss is to God a costly and precious thing. The second is restraint: because the death of His saints is held at so high a price, those who shed their blood answer for it, as Scripture says plainly that He will make inquisition for blood. The verse has accordingly been the martyrs' text in every persecution, read at countless gravesides, and rightly so.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): Precious, of great price; costly; highly valued. Sight, in Scripture, the view or estimation of a person. Precious in the sight of the LORD, Psalm 116:15, the costly value God sets on the death of His saints.
webster_full: Precious, of great price; costly; of great worth or value; highly esteemed.
Sight, view or judgment; in Scripture, the estimation in which one is held.
Hebrew yaqar, costly, weighty, rare, held at a high price.
Hebrew be-einei, in the eyes of, that is, by a particular person's reckoning.
Said of the death of his saints, Hebrew chasidim, his covenant-kept ones.
scriptures: Precious in the sight of the LORD is the death of his saints.
The sorrows of death compassed me, and the pains of hell gat hold upon me: I found trouble and sorrow.

And I heard a voice from heaven saying unto me, Write, Blessed are the dead which die in the Lord from henceforth: Yea, saith the Spirit, that they may rest from their labours; and their works do follow them.
Php 1:21
For to me to live is Christ, and to die is gain.
corruption_summary: The verse is sentimentalized into a general statement that God values all dying, and in some hands bent to commend chosen death, which inverts both the word and the Psalm.
corruption_paragraphs: Read as a comfort for every funeral without distinction, the verse quietly loses the word saints. The Psalm says the death of his saints, the chasidim, those bound to Him in covenant mercy, and Scripture elsewhere is equally plain that the death of the wicked is not so — God has no pleasure in it and calls men to turn and live. A minister who applies the text indiscriminately robs it of the very comfort he means to give, since what consoles the believing is precisely that God values the dying of his own and nobody dies outside that count.

A graver misuse presses the verse toward the approving of death chosen or hastened, as though a precious death might be one a man arranges. The Psalm is the thanksgiving of a man who begged to be delivered from death and was; its author calls his own preservation a loosing of bonds. Scripture reserves the appointing of death to God, forbids the taking of innocent life, and makes the body the Lord's. The principle to recover is the martyr's, not the physician-assisted: a death is precious because God sets the price on it, and the believer's part is to live until He calls and then to depart in peace.
roots_summary: Hebrew yaqar, costly or held at a high price; chasid, one bound in covenant mercy — the dying of such a one is reckoned dear, and blood shed is required.

word: My Flesh and My Heart Faileth
pronunciation: my FLESH and my HART FAY-leth
pos: n. phr. (Asaph's confession of total creaturely failure, answered by God as portion)
etymology: Hebrew kalah she'eri u-levavi — kalah, to be spent, consumed, or brought to an end; she'er, flesh or body; levav, the heart, the seat of mind and will; the margin notes that strength in the next clause is literally rock.
biblical_def: The seventy-third Psalm is Asaph's account of nearly losing his footing over the prosperity of the wicked, and of recovering it in the sanctuary of God when he considered their end. Having seen it, he says: “Whom have I in heaven but thee? and there is none upon earth that I desire beside thee. My flesh and my heart faileth: but God is the strength of my heart, and my portion for ever.” The confession is total and the Hebrew is blunt — both the body and the inner man are spent, used up, coming to an end. Asaph does not soften it, and this is not a complaint but a settled estimate of what a creature is. The conjunction carries the Psalm: but God. The word rendered strength is literally rock, and the word portion is the inheritance-word used of the Levites, who were given no land because the LORD Himself was their portion. So the man whose flesh and heart are failing says that his rock and his estate are God, and the two halves of the verse together are the whole Reformed doctrine of the creature's emptiness and God's all-sufficiency. The Psalm's last words follow naturally: it is good for me to draw near to God.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): Fail, to become deficient; to be insufficient; to decay; to sink. Portion, a part assigned; an inheritance. My flesh and my heart faileth, Psalm 73:26, the creature spent, with God confessed as rock and inheritance.
webster_full: Fail, to become deficient, to sink, to decay, to be wanting or insufficient.
Portion, a part assigned to one; a share; an inheritance or allotment.
Hebrew kalah, to be spent, consumed, finished, brought to an end.
Hebrew tsur, a rock; the margin's reading of ‘strength of my heart’.
Hebrew cheleq, portion or allotted inheritance, as the LORD was the Levites'.
scriptures: My flesh and my heart faileth: but God is the strength of my heart, and my portion for ever.
Whom have I in heaven but thee? and there is none upon earth that I desire beside thee.
Thou shalt guide me with thy counsel, and afterward receive me to glory.
For which cause we faint not; but though our outward man perish, yet the inward man is renewed day by day.
corruption_summary: Therapeutic reading makes the verse a permission to feel depleted and never reaches its conjunction, while a triumphalist reading denies the failing altogether.
corruption_paragraphs: In its therapeutic use the verse becomes a validating of exhaustion: Asaph was burnt out too. The first clause is honestly quoted and the sentence is then abandoned, which leaves a believer with a diagnosis and no remedy. Scripture's own grammar puts the weight on the second clause, and the Psalm reached it only through the sanctuary of God, where Asaph considered the end of the wicked and his envy died. Biblical practice with a spent man is therefore not to settle him in his depletion but to carry him where Asaph went, since what restored him was not a reframing of his feelings but the sight of God as his rock and portion.

The opposite error is the triumphalist one, common wherever the victorious-life teaching is preached, which cannot allow a saint's flesh and heart to fail at all and reads any such confession as defective faith. Asaph is a temple singer under inspiration, and the apostle says the same thing of himself when the outward man perishes while the inward man is renewed day by day. The principle to recover is the honesty of the Psalter. A Christian may say that he is spent and in the same breath that God is his portion for ever, and the two statements do not weaken but establish each other.
roots_summary: Hebrew kalah, to be spent or consumed; tsur, rock, the margin's reading for strength; cheleq, allotted portion — the Levites' inheritance-word applied to God Himself.
